blocks.text: How much damage swarms of locusts inflict on the regions of Syria and Egypt will be better understood from what the writers of histories as well as of travels report to us. GREGORY BARHEBRAEUS, also called ABULPHARAGIUS, in his Chronicle, written in Syriac, copied by Bruns from the Bodleian manuscript and edited by Kirsch, p. 134: [Syriac, 14 lines, not transcribed here] In the year of the Greeks 1095 (which was A.D. 784) flying locusts invaded; they ruined the crops and laid eggs, and those hatched from them, after they had grown wings, climbed the walls and partitions, and entered the houses through the windows and doors [Cf. Exod. X, 6. ומלאו בתיך ובתי כל עבדיך ובתי כל מצרים, the locusts shall fill your houses, and those of your courtiers and subjects]. Water jars, floors, tables and dishes were filled with them. After they had entered the houses from the south side, they went out on the north side, having consumed the grass, the trees, even the woollen clothes and garments of the people. Having laid waste the whole region of Edessa and Sarug, they passed on towards the west. And the continuator of Barhebraeus, in dem Neuen Repertorio für bibl. und morgenl. Literat., edited by Paulus, T. I. p. 67 f.: [Syriac, 10 lines, not transcribed here] In the year 1774 (A.D. 1463) many locusts came from the east, and wingless ones at that [This seems to be how the words ܘܕܒܒܐ ܐܝܬܝܗܘܢ ܗܘܐ should be rendered, which Bruns translated: and flies invaded. But ܕܒܒܐ here undoubtedly agrees in meaning with the Arabic دُبَّاءٌ [dubbāʾ], a locust not yet winged]. They came as far as Egypt; they ate the crops, the vineyards, the fruits, the trees, even the grass, and left nothing green on the face of the earth. The vineyards, fruits and trees failed, stripped and devoured by the locusts. LEO AFRICANUS in the Descript. Africae [III, 284] book 2, ch. 11, p. 77, Zurich edition 1559: When I was staying among them (the people of Tagtessa), a great multitude of locusts had invaded that region, which I would dare to affirm had grown so much that they far exceeded the ears of grain, which had then reached ripeness: so that the very surface of the ground was completely covered with locusts. [Cf. Exod. X, 15. ויכס את עין כל הארץ ותחשך הארץ They covered the whole surface of the earth and darkened it]. And this in the year 919, which was 1510 of Christ. The same Leo, book 9, ch. 61, p. 512: In Africa locusts are usually seen in such numbers that in flight, like a cloud, they cover the rays of the sun. They eat the trees themselves together with their leaves and fruit. When about to depart they leave eggs, from which others (although they do not fly) spring forth, and wherever they are found they eat everything down to the bark of the trees, and leave behind a great scarcity of grain, especially in Mauritania. LE BRUN, Voyages au Levant p. 252, mentions a swarm of locusts which within the space of two hours had consumed everything green, and the places in Cyprus through which these insects had passed were as if devastated by fire. RUSSELL reports the same, Natural History of Aleppo p. 62 (Of the noxious kind may well be reckoned the locust, which sometimes arrive in such incredibile multitudes, that it would appear fabulous to relate, destroying the whole of the verdure where-ever they pass). Whoever wants more may consult OEDMANN in den Vermischten Sammlungen fasc. 2, ch. 6, p. 95 ff., and our Scholia on Exod. X, 14. p. 450 ff., 2nd edition.
In Egypt barley ripens in the month of February; wheat lasts until the end of March, says Forsskål in the Prolegomenn. ad Flor. Aegypt. p. XLIII.
Compare the passage of Barhebraeus cited above, note 1.
